bites.title: Start from the task and its risks, not from the brand
bites.body:
The wrong way to choose is to start with a name: "we should use X, everyone is talking about it". The right way starts with the job.

What exactly must be done? How often? With what data? What happens if the answer is wrong: a small embarrassment, a lost customer, a legal problem? Who is affected?

Those answers set the requirements, and the requirements pick the product.

It is choosing a vehicle. You do not start with the badge. You start with "I need to move six people" or "I need to carry bricks down a muddy track".

A low-risk drafting task and a high-risk customer-facing one may end up on different products from the same shelf.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What should come first when choosing an AI product?

choices.text: The most talked-about brand
The most expensive option
The newest release
A clear description of the task and what happens when it goes wrong

questions.explanation: Requirements come from the task and its risks, and those requirements determine which product fits.

bites.title: Quality on your task, not benchmark rank
bites.body:
The only quality that matters is quality on the work you actually have.

A model can lead the public rankings and still mishandle your trade's abbreviations, your document layout or your tone of voice. A lower-ranked one may suit them well.

So the central piece of evidence in any choice is a test on your own examples. Gather 20 to 50 real cases with the answers you would accept. Run each candidate. Read the results yourself.

It is an audition. A CV tells you who to invite. It does not tell you who gets the part.

Rankings are for the shortlist. The decision comes from the audition.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What is the strongest evidence when comparing AI products for a job?

choices.text: Position on a public leaderboard
The size of the marketing budget
Results on a set of your own real examples
The number of social media followers

questions.explanation: Performance on your own data reflects your real needs, which general rankings cannot.

bites.title: Cost per task, licence, data residency, lock-in, and support
bites.body:
Quality gets the attention. Five quieter criteria decide whether a choice survives contact with reality.

Cost per task: the full cost of one finished job at your volume, not the price per token.

Licence: are you allowed to use it this way, commercially, for this purpose?

Data residency: where is the data processed and stored, and does that meet your obligations?

Lock-in: how hard would it be to leave?

Support: when it breaks on a Friday afternoon, is there someone to call, or only a forum?

It is renting an office. The rooms matter, and so do the lease, the location, the notice period and the landlord. Any one of these can rule out an option that otherwise looks best.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Which of these is a decision criterion alongside quality?

choices.text: The colour of the logo
The length of the product name
How many awards the founder has
Data residency: where the data is processed and stored

questions.explanation: Where data lives, along with cost, licence, lock-in and support, can decide whether a product is usable at all.

bites.title: Speed and reliability: uptime history and rate limits
bites.body:
A brilliant model that is slow or often unavailable makes a poor product.

Speed has two parts. Time to first token: how long before anything appears. Tokens per second: how fast the rest arrives. For chat and voice, the first matters most.

Reliability is about staying up. Providers publish a status page with their record of incidents. Read back a few months before you depend on one.

Rate limits cap how many requests or tokens you may send per minute. New accounts start low. A limit that is fine in testing can throttle you on launch day.

Think of a supplier. Quality counts, and so does delivering on time, every time, in the quantity you ordered.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Where can you check how often a provider's service has had outages?

choices.text: On a benchmark leaderboard
In its model card
On its public status page and incident history
In its logo

questions.explanation: Status pages record past incidents, which is the direct evidence of reliability.

bites.title: Features you need: tool use, long context, vision, structured output
bites.body:
Models differ in what they can do, not only in how well. Before comparing quality, check that the candidate has the features your task needs.

Tool use: can it reliably call functions to fetch data and take actions? This is essential for agents.

Long context: can it take your largest documents in one request?

Vision: can it read images, scans and screenshots?

Structured output: can it be made to return exactly the format, such as JSON, that your software expects?

Others include audio, prompt caching, batch pricing and fine-tuning.

It is a pre-flight checklist. If one must-have is missing, the option is out, whatever its score. Write the must-haves down before you start looking.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Which feature is essential for a model that will power an agent?

choices.text: The longest product name
Image generation
Reliable tool use
The lowest possible price

questions.explanation: Agents work by calling tools, so dependable function calling is a must-have for that role.

bites.title: Score two or three finalists on the same test set
bites.body:
The end of the selection is a fair contest. Take two or three finalists and run each one on exactly the same examples, with the same instructions.

Then record the same measures for each: how many answers were acceptable, the cost per task, the time taken, and the kinds of mistake made.

Put the results in a simple table. The decision usually becomes obvious, and it is now documented.

It is a blind tasting. Same glasses, same conditions, and the labels are hidden until the scores are written down.

Two warnings. Do not test one model on easy cases and another on hard ones. And do not judge on a single run, because outputs vary. Run each case several times.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: What makes a comparison between finalist models fair?

choices.text: Giving each model a different set of questions
Running each on the same examples with the same instructions and measures
Testing each once on one easy case
Choosing in advance and testing only that one

questions.explanation: Identical test conditions isolate the difference between the models from the difference between the tests.
